column5: law written on hearts
column6: Alongside the commentary's word kept in an instructed memory and in written pages, Jeremiah promises that God will write the law on the people's hearts, giving an explicit inward-inscription image.

column5: scroll written on both sides
column6: Ezekiel sees a scroll covered on front and back with lamentation and woe; it adds a concrete written surface and prophetic warning to the commentary's individual pages.

column5: prophet eats the scroll before speaking
column6: Ezekiel must eat the written scroll and then speak to Israel, joining page, mouth, and delivered warning in a way that complements the commentary's recited pages and remembered word.

column5: Moses completes the written law
column6: Deuteronomy says Moses finished writing the words of the law in a book; this supplies the act of making the written witness that the commentary distinguishes from separate pages.

column5: Moses' teaching falls like rain on grass
column6: In Moses' song, teaching is rain and speech dew that falls on grass and plants; this is a particular meeting of the commentary's Musa, recited word, and pasture imagery.

column5: Moses' song says God kills and makes alive
column6: The same song declares that God kills and gives life, a direct Mosaic-scripture counterpart to the life-and-death claim the commentary finds among the old pages.

column5: word goes out and accomplishes its purpose
column6: Isaiah says God's word does not return empty but achieves its work; beside the commentary's withering pasture and enduring pages, the verse makes the written warning effective, not merely preserved.

column5: Abraham calls on the Lord's name and worships
column6: After arriving in Canaan, Abraham builds an altar and calls on the Lord's name; this is a concrete patriarchal instance of the commentary's remembered name joined to prayer.

column5: Pharaoh claims the Nile as his creation
column6: Ezekiel depicts Pharaoh boasting that the Nile is his and that he made it, while the commentary sets Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord against the true creator; this gives the same arrogance a specifically Egyptian form.

column5: God brings every deed, even hidden ones, to judgment
column6: Ecclesiastes says every work and hidden thing will be brought to judgment; this sharpens the commentary's reading of the pages as a record of each person's striving and recompense.

column5: God weighs the heart and repays each person
column6: Proverbs says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each according to deeds; this closely matches the commentary's reading that labor is seen and no one answers for another.

column5: Moses speaks of God's book
column6: Moses asks to be blotted from God's book if Israel is not forgiven; this gives the commentary's book held with God a Mosaic setting, though Exodus uses it as a book of life rather than a record of the first generations.

column5: old events written as warning for the end
column6: Paul says Israel's past events happened as examples and were written for admonition in the age's end; this directly matches the commentary's claim that the first pages remain a warning to present rejecters.

column5: earlier writings instruct and give hope
column6: Paul says what was written beforehand was written for instruction and endurance; this Christian reading makes the commentary's old pages a present source of admonition and hope.

column5: earthly comfort reversed after death
column6: Abraham tells the rich man that he received good things in life while Lazarus suffered, but now their conditions are reversed; this is a close parable counterpart to preferring the lasting afterlife over worldly life.

column5: fixed chasm after judgment
column6: Abraham says a great chasm prevents crossing between the two conditions; this adds the finality of the commentary's divided destinies after the present choice.

column5: two final outcomes, punishment and life
column6: Jesus ends the judgment scene with eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other; this closely matches the commentary's contrast between the rejecter and the successful person.

column5: Scriptures testify about the messenger
column6: Jesus says the Scriptures bear witness to him; this expands the nearby claim that Moses wrote about him and parallels the commentary's pages testifying to a warning delivered anew.

column5: Moses and prophets interpreted as pointing forward
column6: The risen Jesus interprets Moses and all the prophets from the Scriptures concerning himself; this is a Christian reading of earlier writings as a unified witness to a later message.

column5: Moses, prophets, and psalms fulfilled together
column6: Jesus names the Law of Moses, Prophets, and Psalms as writings that must be fulfilled; this supplies a distinct Christian account of separate earlier texts converging in one message.

column5: Moses refuses Pharaoh's household identity
column6: Hebrews says Moses refused to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son; this adds a specific act of rejecting the status of Pharaoh's house to the commentary's contrast between false lordship and allegiance to God.

column5: Moses leaves without fearing the king
column6: Hebrews says Moses left Egypt by faith without fearing the king's anger; this complements the commentary's link between fear, guidance, and the choice to obey God's warning.

column5: resurrection to life or judgment
column6: Jesus distinguishes resurrection of life from resurrection of judgment; it gives a specific Christian statement of the two outcomes that the commentary locates in the old pages.

column5: sealed scroll written inside and out
column6: Revelation shows a scroll written on both sides and sealed, a direct textual object parallel to the commentary's sheets and an apocalyptic contrast between preserved writing and its opening.

column5: scroll eaten, sweet in the mouth and bitter within
column6: John eats the little scroll and experiences its divided taste; with Ezekiel's eaten scroll, this adds a Christian apocalyptic image of written revelation becoming inward speech and burden.

column5: deeds follow the dead
column6: The heavenly voice says the dead are blessed and their deeds follow them; this gives a precise Christian counterpart to the pages' claim that each person's effort is seen and carried into recompense.

column5: Scripture announces good news beforehand to Abraham
column6: Paul says Scripture foresaw the nations being justified and announced the good news beforehand to Abraham; this interprets the patriarch's earlier witness as carrying a message for later peoples.

column5: Abraham's trust counted as righteousness
column6: Paul reads Abraham's belief in Genesis as the basis of being counted righteous; this is a distinct Christian interpretation of the patriarch named in the first pages.

column5: Abraham's offering of Isaac as an act of faith
column6: James recalls Abraham offering Isaac and says the patriarch was justified by works; this connects the commentary's Abraham as one who fulfilled with a concrete Christian account of faithful action.

column5: faith completed through works
column6: James says Abraham's faith worked with his deeds and was brought to completion by them; beside Paul's reading of Abraham's trust, it preserves a second Christian interpretation of his faithfulness.

column5: ancestors reject Moses and turn back to Egypt
column6: Stephen says the ancestors refused Moses and turned back in their hearts toward Egypt; this gives a scriptural counterexample to relying on ancestors when their path rejects the messenger.

column5: claiming Abraham while opposing Abraham's way
column6: Jesus says his hearers seek to kill him although he told them truth from God, unlike Abraham; this develops the commentary's distinction between naming the patriarch and following his conduct.

column5: opponents corrected gently toward repentance
column6: Paul instructs a servant of the Lord to correct opponents with gentleness in hope that God grants repentance; this Christian counsel is a specific ethical counterpart to Moses being told to address Pharaoh softly.

column5: king refuses to fear after hearing the scroll
column6: After hearing Jeremiah's scroll, the king and servants show no fear and do not tear their clothes; this is a concrete counter-scene to the commentary's claim that the hearer who fears takes the admonition to heart.

column5: rain makes the earth sprout
column6: Isaiah's rain and snow water the earth and make it yield seed and bread; this specific image meets the commentary's pasture and its concern with a word that remains effective.

column5: new heart replaces the heart of stone
column6: Ezekiel promises a new heart and spirit in place of a heart of stone; this adds a prophetic image of inward receptivity to the commentary's preserved word in memory.

column5: the prophet speaks whether hearers listen or refuse
column6: Ezekiel is told that the rebellious may hear or refuse but must know a prophet was among them; this differs from the surah's conditional reminder and Musa's hope that Pharaoh may remember or fear.

column5: soft answer turns away wrath
column6: The proverb says a gentle answer turns away anger; this gives a wisdom-text counterpart to Moses being commanded to speak gently to Pharaoh.

column5: righteous memory is a blessing
column6: Proverbs contrasts the blessed remembrance of the righteous with the decaying name of the wicked; this adds a wisdom formulation for the commentary's names of Abraham and Moses preserved among later people.

column5: one generation tells the next of God's works
column6: The psalm says one generation praises God's works to another; it gives a concrete liturgical practice for the later remembrance that closes the commentary's account of Abraham and Moses.

column5: awakening to life or disgrace
column6: Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening to everlasting life or disgrace; this adds a Hebrew-scriptural resurrection scene to the commentary's final distinction of outcomes.

column5: Abraham rejoices to see Jesus' day
column6: Jesus says Abraham rejoiced to see his day; this is a distinct Christian interpretation of Abraham as one whose earlier story reaches toward a later messenger.

column5: Torah transmitted from Moses onward
column6: The Mishnah traces reception from Moses to Joshua, elders, prophets, and later teachers; it gives a Jewish model for the named Mosaic revelation reaching later generations.

column5: books opened for the year's judgment
column6: The Talmud interprets divine judgment through books opened for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate; this develops the commentary's opened pages and divided human outcomes.

column5: heavenly books opened before the judge
column6: Enoch sees the books of the living opened before the heavenly court; this Jewish apocalyptic scene develops the commentary's old record as witness at judgment.

column5: Enoch reads the heavenly tablets
column6: Enoch is shown written heavenly tablets and instructed to read and record what they contain; this is a close pseudepigraphal counterpart to Moses' book of the first generations kept with God.

column5: Abraham refuses idolatry and faces the furnace
column6: The Targumic retelling connects Abraham's origin in Ur with refusal of an idol and the fiery ordeal; it adds an Aramaic Jewish version of the ancestral break developed in the commentary.

column5: Abraham rejects the idols of his father's house
column6: This pseudepigraphal account expands Abraham's confrontation with his father's idols; it gives another Jewish setting for the commentary's claim that the first pages belong to one who leaves ancestral worship.

column5: Abraham's obedience in leaving his homeland
column6: Clement recalls Abraham as faithful and obedient when he left his country; this early Christian interpretation turns the patriarch's departure into a model of trusting the divine call.
